title: Raga Bilaval
hookLine: a morning raga of joy that opens with a praise-singer admitting his words are too small, and singing on

cards: Calling a king sir is not a compliment. It's a downgrade. Sir is what you call the man at the next table, and leaving off a king's bigger titles is a little insult, however politely it's meant.
Now turn to where a new raga begins in the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Nanak opens it with exactly that problem: every title he has is too small for the One he's singing to. And he sings on anyway.

teach.b: First, the place. Bilaval follows Suhi in the Granth's order. Sikh tradition, along with the wider music it grew from, links Bilaval with morning and joy.

teach.h: YOU ARE THE SULTAN; I SAY SIR.
teach.b: Second, the opening line, in paraphrase: you are the Sultan; if I call you Mian, sir, what greatness is that? Mian was a respectful title in Guru Nanak's world.
Beside the One who made everything, it's like calling the ocean a puddle. Third, the confession. Whatever you give, Master, that is what I say; I'm a fool, I can't find the words.
Then the refrain, a request: give me understanding, so I can sing your praises and live in truth, by your will. Then: whatever has happened has come from you; you know everything.
I can't know your limit, my Master; what cleverness do I have?

teach.h: I SPEAK, AND IT CAN'T BE SAID.
teach.b: I speak and speak, and see that the one beyond words can't be put into words. Whatever pleases you, I say, and it's a sesame seed of your greatness. Fourth, the joy.
A praise song that keeps admitting it can't praise might sound like defeat. But it doesn't stop; it asks for understanding to keep singing, in a raga tradition links with joy. There's freedom in it.
Nobody has to find the perfect word, because it doesn't exist.

teach.h: TOO BIG FOR WORDS, SUNG GLADLY.
teach.b: So the morning song can start with a small one, sir, smile at how small it is, and still be sung gladly.

how: Shabads from the Bilaval section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Bilaval, which Sikh musical tradition links with the morning and a joyful mood.

o: a raga for evening songs of loss and longing
the morning raga after Suhi, linked with joy
the raga of the yogis and their begging bags

games.q: inside Bilaval's first hymn — tap the pairs.

s: Bilaval's first hymn finds the perfect title for God
it calls the Sultan sir and admits every title is too small.
tradition links Bilaval with morning and joy
Sikh musical tradition, and the wider music it grew from, hear Bilaval as a joyful morning raga.
the singer stops singing because words fall short
he keeps singing: I speak and speak, and see it can't be said.

games.q: you're singing praise, and every title you know is too small. what do you do?
o: stop, until you find a big enough word.
admit the words fall short, and keep singing gladly.
games.why: Guru Nanak says: you are the Sultan; if I call you sir, what greatness is that? then he sings on, in a raga of morning joy.

practice: Choose something larger than you, the sky this morning, the ocean, the fact that you woke up at all, and try to describe it in a few words in your head.

Notice how small the words are and let it be a little funny, the way sir is funny for a sultan; then let the words go and enjoy the thing itself, with one Waheguru if you pray, or a small smile if you don't.

wordCard.voice: Raga Bilaval. The raga after Suhi, linked by tradition with morning and joy, which opens with Guru Nanak calling the Sultan sir and singing on anyway. Today's word.
